lessons.title: ein / eine: a place in the city
lessons.goal: Name places in a city and say what a thing is, with ein or eine.

grammar.point: ein for der-words and das-words; eine for die-words; no ein for many things
grammar.oneLine: der → ein, das → ein, die → eine. Many things: no ein.

mistake.why: Bank is a die-word, so it takes eine.

terms.meaning: a or an: the word for one thing that is new
the little word for a or an: ein or eine
the little word for the: der, die or das
those are: the plural of das ist

cards.title: Before we start: places in a city
cards.body: You step off the train in Hamburg and see a big building. What is it? Chapter 3 is about the city: places, getting around, directions and the seasons. Today you point and say what a thing is, like a first sign on a map.
steps: You already know: der, die, das from chapter 2
New today: ein and eine, which mean a or an
By the end you can: say Das ist ein Hotel or Das ist eine Kirche

examples.why: New today: ein means a. The gender still decides.
New today: a die-word needs eine.

cards.more: Think of a city map with little labels. Until now you used the, for something you both know. A is for something new: Look, a church! German has a small a-word for each gender, so ein and eine are like name tags that match der, die and das. You do not have to guess. You will meet the word, then the table, then practise, step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: Was ist das? Das ist ein …
cards.body: To say what a thing is, use Das ist ein … and then the noun. ein means a or an. Ask with Was ist das? The verb ist is always part 2.
steps: Point at it: Was ist das?
cards.more: Picture yourself on a walk. You point at a big building and your friend asks: Was ist das? You answer with a small pattern. Step 1: say Das ist. Step 2: say ein, like the English word a. Step 3: say the place. Das ist ein Kino. The verb ist stays in part 2, just like in chapter 1. Extra example: Das ist ein Park. = That is a park.
cards.lead: The intro showed a station and a hotel in Hamburg. On this card: how to point at a place and say what it is with the word ein, so you can name things you see in town.

deeper.text: In German, Das ist ein Bahnhof is a complete sentence, and ist can never be left out. Notice also that das is the same word for every noun. You point first with das, and only the noun that follows shows its gender. That is why you do not need to know the gender before you point at something.

cards.title: A die-word needs eine
cards.body: A noun with die takes eine, with an e on the end. The noun does not change. die Bank becomes eine Bank. The ending -e on ein shows that the noun is a die-word.
cards.more: Think of ein as a plain T-shirt and eine as the same T-shirt with a little badge: the e. Only the die-words wear the badge. So the question is always the same: is it a die-word? Step 1: look at the noun: die Bank. Step 2: die means badge, so eine. Step 3: say it. Extra example: Das ist eine Uhr. = That is a clock. (die Uhr)
cards.lead: You just saw ein for der-words and das-words. On this card: the die-word exception, where ein gets an -e to become eine, so you can say Bank or Kirche correctly.

deeper.text: Say eine out loud: the final -e is a short, soft sound, like the end of Kirche. Here is a handy clue. Many nouns that end in -e, such as Kirche or Schule (school), are die-words. It is a clue, not a law, but it works very often, so look at the ending when you learn a new noun.

cards.title: The table: der, die, das → ein, eine, ein
cards.body: Learn the three together. der and das both become ein. Only die becomes eine. So you look at the word for the, then pick: der → ein, das → ein, die → eine.
cards.more: Here is the secret: you only need to remember one odd thing. der and das share the same a-word, ein. Only die is different. Step 1: ask yourself: der, die or das? Step 2: der or das? Say ein. Step 3: die? Add the e and say eine. That is the whole system. Extra example: das Foto becomes ein Foto. der Computer becomes ein Computer.
cards.lead: Now you know ein and eine. On this card: all three genders side by side, so you can pick the right form for any place word without guessing.

deeper.text: Look at what really changes in the table: only the little word before the noun. The noun itself stays exactly the same. Notice that eine tells you die for sure. But ein could belong to a der-word or a das-word, so ein hides the gender. This is why you learn every noun together with der, die or das.

cards.title: The or a? Known and new
cards.body: Say ein for a new thing, the first time. Say der, die or das when you talk about that same thing again. You both know it now.
cards.more: In English it is the same: I see a dog. The dog is big. First it is a dog, a stranger. Then it is the dog, because you both know it. German does it the same way. Step 1: new thing? Use ein or eine. Step 2: talk about it again? Use der, die or das. Extra example: Das ist eine Kirche. Die Kirche ist alt.
cards.lead: You can now say a for something new. On this card: when to keep ein for the first mention and switch to der, die or das once you talk about the same place again.

deeper.text: English does the same: a park first, then the park. The difference is that German must also choose der, die or das for the second mention, so the gender matters again. Also notice what usually happens: the first sentence introduces a thing, and the next sentence says something about it, like it is new or old.

cards.title: Many things: no ein
cards.body: ein means one. So there is no ein for many things. For many, use no article and sind: Das sind Kinos. The plural endings are the ones from chapter 2. Ask: Was sind das?

examples.why: die Bank has the plural Banken.

cards.more: ein is like the number one. You cannot say one cinemas. So for many cinemas you drop it. Step 1: one thing? Das ist ein Kino. Step 2: many things? Das sind Kinos. The verb changes too: ist for one, sind for many. Extra example: Das ist ein Park. Das sind Parks.
cards.lead: So far every sentence named one thing. On this card: what to say for several places, with sind and no ein, so you can talk about a few banks or parks.

deeper.text: Why no ein for many things? Because ein really means one, so it cannot stand before several things. English does the same: a cinema, but cinemas. Notice two more changes. The verb becomes sind, because it matches the number. And das stays das even for many things. You say Das sind Kinos, never Die sind Kinos.

cards.title: Find the form in 3 steps
cards.body: When you are not sure, use three steps. They work for every place in this lesson.
cards.more: Think of a recipe with three steps. Step 1: find the gender of the noun. Learn it with the noun: der Markt, die Kirche, das Rathaus. Step 2: der or das gives ein. die gives eine. Step 3: put it together: Das ist ein Markt. If you learn the article with every noun, this is easy. Extra example: Das ist ein Hotel. = That is a hotel.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: a three-step check you can use for any place, so you can choose ein or eine every time.

deeper.text: The middle step does all the work: find the word for the. A der-word like Hafen and a das-word like Museum both give ein, and only a die-word gives something different, eine. So never learn a noun alone. Learn it with its der, die or das, and the right a-word follows by itself.

lessons.title: kein / keine: not a
lessons.goal: Say that something is not a place, with kein, keine and nicht.

grammar.point: kein for der- and das-words, keine for die-words and many things; nicht for describing words
grammar.oneLine: ein → kein, eine → keine. Many things: keine. A describing word: nicht.

mistake.why: Before a noun with ein, German uses kein. It does not use nicht ein.

terms.meaning: a word that says no: kein, keine, nicht
not a, no: ein and eine with a k in front
not: it stands before a describing word
a word like neu or müde that says what something is like

cards.title: Before we start: saying what is not there
cards.body: A friend asks: Is that a cinema? It is not. You need a short way to say not a. Today you add one little k to what you know, and you can say no to a place.
steps: You already know: ein and eine from the last lesson
New today: kein and keine mean not a
By the end you can: say Das ist kein Kino
cards.more: Imagine ein is a little sticker saying a. To say not a, you add a k at the front, like a small stop sign: ein turns into kein, eine into keine. That is the whole trick. There is also nicht for describing words, and you will learn when to use which. Take it one card at a time; each card adds just one small piece.

cards.title: kein: not a
cards.body: kein means not a or no. Put it where ein stood. You often say it after nein, and then you say what the thing really is.

examples.en: No, that is not a cinema.

examples.why: Now say what it is: ein Museum.
Yes/no question: the verb is first.

cards.more: Imagine a friend points at a building and says: a cinema? You say no. English says: that is not a cinema. German adds a k to ein and makes kein. Step 1: say nein. Step 2: say Das ist. Step 3: say kein and the noun. Step 4: say what it really is. Extra example: Das ist kein Park. Das ist ein Markt.
cards.lead: In lesson 1 you learned ein and eine for a thing. On this card: kein, the word for not a, and how it answers a yes/no question about a place, so you can say no.

deeper.text: kein is really nicht and ein squeezed into one word, a bit like English no in no cinema. Before a noun, German does not say nicht ein. It says kein. Also notice the pattern of a normal conversation: after you say what it is not, you usually add what it really is, so the listener is not left guessing.

example.en: No, that is not a park.

cards.title: kein for der-words and das-words
cards.body: For a der-word or a das-word, ein becomes kein. Just add a k in front. The noun does not change.
cards.more: A der-word and a das-word are twins for ein, and they are twins for kein too. Step 1: find the noun and its article: der Markt or das Hotel. Step 2: der or das? Then use ein for yes. Step 3: for no, put a k in front of ein: kein. That is all. Extra example: Das ist kein Hafen. = That is not a harbour.
cards.lead: You now have a no-word for one thing. On this card: how ein turns into kein for der-words and das-words, so you can say a station or hotel is not there.

deeper.text: Both der-words and das-words give kein, so kein does not show you the gender. Pronunciation tip: kein rhymes with English mine, just like ein. The only new thing is the k at the front, a short hard sound. Everything else stays as it was: the noun, the verb and the word order do not change at all.

cards.title: keine for die-words
cards.body: For a die-word, eine becomes keine. Again just add a k in front. The ending -e stays.
cards.more: Remember the badge from the last lesson: eine had a little e. With keine you keep the badge and add a k in front of the whole word. Step 1: find the noun: die Bank. Step 2: die? Then yes is eine. Step 3: no is keine. Say it: Das ist keine Bank. Extra example: Das ist keine Brücke. = That is not a bridge.
cards.lead: The der and das form is clear now. On this card: the die-word version, where eine becomes keine and the -e stays, so you can say not a bank or not a church.

deeper.text: keine is not a new idea. It is just kein plus the -e that eine already had. So you can always build the no-form from the yes-form: put a k in front. ein becomes kein, eine becomes keine. If you can say the yes-sentence, you can say the no-sentence, and you never need a separate list.

cards.title: keine for many things, and the whole set
cards.body: For many things, use keine too, with sind. Look at the whole set: der-word kein, die-word keine, das-word kein, many things keine.
cards.more: Many things have no ein, but for no you still need a word. That word is keine. It is like a single word that works for every die-word and for all the plurals. Step 1: many things? Say Das sind. Step 2: add keine. Step 3: add the plural noun. Extra example: Das sind keine Kinos. = Those are not cinemas.
cards.lead: You have three singular forms of kein. On this card: all four forms side by side, plus keine for many things with sind, so you can say those are not parks.

deeper.text: ein has no plural, because it means one. But kein does have one: keine. It means not any, or simply no. Das sind keine Hotels means Those are not hotels. English works the same way: no banks here. So for many things, keine is the normal no-word, and the noun stays in its plural form.

cards.title: nicht or kein?
cards.body: kein goes with a noun that had ein or no article. nicht goes with a describing word like neu or müde. nicht stands right before it. Both mean not.
cards.more: Ask yourself one question: what do I say no to? If it is a thing, a noun with ein, use kein. If it is a description, like new or tired, use nicht. Step 1: look at the word after ist or bin. Step 2: a noun? kein. Step 3: a word like neu or müde? nicht. Extra example: Der Park ist nicht alt. = The park is not old.
cards.lead: Kein only goes with nouns, and you have seen it in all forms. On this card: when to use nicht instead, for a describing word like neu or müde, so you pick the right not.

deeper.text: Here is a quick test. Could you put ein or eine in front of the word? Or is it a plural with no article? Then use kein or keine. If it is a describing word instead, use nicht. Keep this test in your head. It decides between the two nots almost every time, so you do not have to guess.

cards.title: Answer yes or no
cards.body: A yes/no question starts with the verb. Answer with ja or nein and a full sentence. For no, use kein or keine.

examples.en: No, that is not a cinema.

cards.more: A good answer is short and complete. Step 1: say ja or nein. Step 2: say the full sentence with Das ist. Step 3: for ja use ein or eine. For nein use kein or keine. If the question is about many things, ask Sind das …? and answer Das sind keine … Extra example: Ist das eine Bank? Nein, das ist keine Bank.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: how to answer a yes/no question with ja or nein and a full sentence, so you can say no with kein or keine.

deeper.text: Real Germans sometimes answer very short, like Nein, kein Kino. In this course, try to say the full sentence anyway. It trains the verb in part 2, and that habit helps in every later lesson. Also notice that nein is followed by a comma, and the real answer comes right after it.

example.en: No, that is not a bank.

lessons.title: Getting around: transport and Wo ist …?
lessons.goal: Say how you travel and ask where a place is.

grammar.point: Transport is a whole piece: mit dem Bus, mit der U-Bahn, zu Fuß; ask Wo ist …? and answer with hier, da, dort
grammar.oneLine: Learn mit dem Bus as one piece. fahren = by vehicle, gehen = on foot.

mistake.why: The piece is mit dem Bus. Do not drop dem.

terms.meaning: the way you travel: bus, train, bike
a group of words you learn together, like mit dem Bus
on foot: one piece
here / there / over there

cards.title: Before we start: getting around
cards.body: You want to go to the harbour. Bus, train or on foot? And where is the station? Today you say how you travel and ask where a place is, the first steps of finding your way.
steps: You already know: the verb is part 2 from chapter 1
New today: mit dem Bus, mit der U-Bahn, zu Fuß as whole pieces
By the end you can: say how you travel and ask Wo ist …?

examples.why: New today: mit dem Bus is one piece. The verb is still part 2.

cards.more: Think of ways to travel as little luggage tags. mit dem Bus, mit der U-Bahn, mit dem Zug: each is a small box you carry whole, so you do not take it apart. You just learn the box and drop it into a sentence you know already. The verb stays in its place, in part 2. You will practise a few boxes at a time in the next cards.

cards.title: How do you travel? Wie fährst du?
cards.body: Ask Wie fährst du? Answer with Ich fahre mit dem Bus. mit dem Bus is one piece: learn it whole. Why it is dem comes in chapter 7. The verb fahren is still part 2.
steps: Add the piece: mit dem Bus
cards.more: You already know fahren from chapter 2: ich fahre, du fährst. Now we say how. Think of mit dem Bus as a ticket that you cannot tear apart. Step 1: ask Wie fährst du? Step 2: answer Ich fahre. Step 3: add the ticket: mit dem Bus. Do not leave out dem. Extra example: Ich fahre mit dem Auto. = I go by car.
cards.lead: You can now name places and say what they are not. On this card: how to ask Wie fährst du? and answer with a travel piece, so you can say how you get around.

deeper.text: fahren changes its vowel with du and er: ich fahre, du fährst, er fährt. The a becomes ä. It is a small irregular pattern, and you will meet more verbs that do the same. Notice that the other forms stay normal. Only du and er/sie change, so watch for the two dots when you read.

cards.title: Ways to travel: learn each as one piece
cards.body: Six ways to travel. Learn each piece whole, with its little words. You will see dem and der. Do not worry why. That comes in chapter 7. For now, copy the piece.
cards.more: Think of a phone book of pieces. Each piece is a ready-made block: mit dem Bus, mit der U-Bahn, mit dem Zug, mit dem Fahrrad, mit dem Auto. You do not build them from small parts today. You just pick the block you need. Say each one out loud three times. Extra example: Anna fährt mit dem Zug. = Anna goes by train.
cards.lead: You just learned fahren for travelling. On this card: six ways to get around, each learned as one whole piece with its little words, so you can say how you go.

deeper.text: mit means with, so mit dem Bus is literally with the bus. English splits it the same way: by bus, but on foot. German says mit for vehicles and zu Fuß for walking. Fuß means foot, so zu Fuß is literally to foot. Treat each piece as one block and you will say it without thinking.

cards.title: On foot: gehen and zu Fuß
cards.body: fahren is for a bus, train, bike or car. gehen is for walking. Say zu Fuß gehen. gehen is a regular verb: take off -en and add the endings from chapter 1.
cards.more: In English you go by bus and you go on foot. German uses two different verbs. If something carries you, use fahren. If your own feet do the work, use gehen. Step 1: ride or walk? Step 2: pick fahren or gehen. Step 3: add the piece: mit dem Bus or zu Fuß. gehen is easy: it follows the normal pattern. Extra example: Er geht zu Fuß. = He walks.
cards.lead: You can say how you travel by bus, train or car. On this card: gehen for walking and zu Fuß, plus how gehen changes for each person, so you can say you walk.

deeper.text: Look at the table again: er geht and ihr geht are the same, and wir gehen and sie gehen are the same. Context tells you who is meant. The same sharing happens in every regular verb, so it is not a trap. Only ich gehe and du gehst are different from the others.

cards.title: Start with the transport: the verb stays second
cards.body: You can start with mit dem Zug. Then the verb must still be part 2, so ich moves behind it. Same meaning, other chair order.

examples.de: Ich fahre mit dem Zug nach Hamburg.
examples.en: I go to Hamburg by train.

examples.de: Mit dem Zug fahre ich nach Hamburg.
examples.en: By train I go to Hamburg.
examples.why: Chair 1 is mit dem Zug. The verb is still part 2.

examples.de: Fährst du mit dem Zug nach Hamburg?
examples.en: Do you go to Hamburg by train?
examples.why: Yes/no question: the verb is first.

cards.more: Remember the chairs from chapter 1. The verb always sits on chair 2. Chair 1 can be ich, but it can also be a whole piece like mit dem Zug. Step 1: pick what goes first. Step 2: put the verb next. Step 3: put the rest after it. Nothing else changes. Extra example: Mit dem Bus fahre ich nach Berlin. = By bus I go to Berlin.
cards.lead: You can ask and answer about travel. On this card: putting the transport words first while the verb stays in second place, so your sentences still sound natural.

deeper.text: Why would you start with mit dem Zug? To give it the spotlight. The first place in a German sentence gets the most attention: By train I go, not by bus. The verb never moves from part 2. Only the other pieces swap around it. Do not put the verb back in a different place.

example.de: Mit dem Auto fährt Ben nach Hamburg.
example.en: Ben goes to Hamburg by car.

cards.title: Where is it? Wo ist …? hier, da, dort
cards.body: Ask Wo ist …? The verb ist is part 2 and the thing comes after it. Answer with hier (here), da (there) or dort (over there). For many things, ask Wo sind …?
cards.more: Imagine you have a toy. Hier is when it is in your hand. Da is when it is on the table next to you. Dort is when it is across the room. Step 1: ask Wo ist? Step 2: say the thing. Step 3: answer with hier, da or dort. Many things need sind: Wo sind die Busse? Extra example: Hier ist ein Taxi. = Here is a taxi.
cards.lead: Next: finding places. On this card: the question Wo ist …? and three small words for near and far, hier, da and dort, so you can say where something is.

deeper.text: In everyday speech, da is often used for both there and here, so you will hear it a lot. hier means close to me, and dort means over there. The verb still stays in part 2 when the answer word comes first. Hier ist die Bank has the verb second, just like Die Bank ist hier.

cards.title: Ask and answer: put it together
cards.body: Now join the pieces. Ask Wie fährst du? and answer with fahren or gehen. Ask Wo ist …? and answer with hier, da or dort. All verbs stay in part 2.

examples.de: Wie fährt Anna? Sie fährt mit der U-Bahn.
examples.en: How does Anna travel? She goes by underground.

examples.de: Wo ist das Taxi? Da ist das Taxi.
examples.en: Where is the taxi? The taxi is there.
examples.why: da at chair 1: the verb is still part 2.

examples.de: Wie gehst du? Ich gehe zu Fuß.
examples.en: How do you go? I walk.

steps: Wie fährst du? Ich fahre mit dem Bus.
Wie fährt Mira? Mit der U-Bahn.
cards.more: A question and an answer are like a ping-pong game. The question hits one word, the answer sends it back. How do you travel? I go by bus. Where is it? Over there. Step 1: look at the question word: wie or wo. Step 2: pick the answer: for wie, a piece like mit dem Bus. For wo, a word like dort. Extra example: Wo ist die U-Bahn? Dort ist die U-Bahn.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: you join travel and places, asking how someone goes and where something is, so you can handle a simple talk about getting around.

deeper.text: Questions with Wo and Wie work the same way: the question word first, then the verb in part 2, then the rest. That is one pattern for all of them. In real life short answers like Dort. or Mit dem Bus. are normal, but a full sentence is the better practice for part 2.

lessons.title: Describe places: sein + adjective
lessons.goal: Say what a place is like, with sein and an adjective.

grammar.point: After sein, the adjective has no ending; nicht, sehr and zu stand right before it
grammar.oneLine: Der Hafen ist groß. No ending after sein.

mistake.why: After sein the adjective never gets an ending.

terms.meaning: a describing word that says what something is like: groß, alt, schön
very: it goes right before an adjective
too, before an adjective
a word that means the reverse: groß and klein

cards.title: Before we start: describing places
cards.body: Your friend asks: What is the harbour like? Big? Loud? Today you learn to describe a place with a short, easy pattern. It is one of the simplest things in German.
steps: You already know: sein (bin, bist, ist) from chapter 1
New today: sein plus a describing word, with no ending
By the end you can: say Der Hafen ist groß

examples.why: New today: the same pattern describes a place.

cards.more: Imagine sein as an equals sign. On the left is the thing, on the right how it is: The harbour = big. You already did this with Ich bin müde. Here the describing word does not change at all, whatever you describe. That makes it easy. You will learn a few opposites, then words like very and too, step by step.

cards.title: Say what a place is like: sein + adjective
cards.body: A describing word is called an adjective. It says what something is like: big, old, nice. Put the adjective after sein. The verb is still part 2.
cards.more: You know sein from chapter 1: Ben ist nett. nett was an adjective already! Now we use the same pattern for places. Step 1: say the thing: der Hafen. Step 2: say ist. Step 3: say the describing word: groß. Think of ist as an equals sign: harbour = big. Extra example: Der Park ist klein. = The park is small.
cards.lead: You can now name places and get around them. On this card: how sein plus a describing word says what a place is like, so you can describe a city or a harbour.

deeper.text: In English you can say a big harbour, with the adjective before the noun. Here it comes after ist: Der Hafen ist groß. This is the pattern to learn first, because it needs no ending at all. Later you will also put adjectives before a noun, and then they do get endings. Not yet.

cards.title: After sein, the adjective has no ending
cards.body: After sein, the adjective never changes. groß stays groß for der-words, die-words, das-words and for many things. Only sein changes: ist for one, sind for many.
cards.more: In English you say: a big park, big parks, the park is big. The word big never changes. German is the same after sein, so this is the easy part. Step 1: pick the adjective. Step 2: do not touch it. Step 3: pick ist or sind. Later, in front of a noun, adjectives get an ending. That is for a later chapter. Not today. Extra example: Das Hotel ist klein. Die Hotels sind klein.
cards.lead: You just saw describing words after ist. On this card: why the describing word never changes after sein, even for die-words, das-words or many things, so you do not add endings.

deeper.text: This is good news: one pattern and no endings to remember. English does the same thing: the park is big, and the parks are big. The adjective stays the same, and only ist or sind changes. So you can describe a der-word, a die-word, a das-word or many things with the very same adjective.

cards.title: Opposites help you learn
cards.body: Learn adjectives in pairs. Two words that mean the opposite are easy to remember together. Say the pair out loud.

examples.why: ruhig = quiet, the opposite of laut.

examples.de: Die Brücke ist alt, aber der Turm ist neu.
examples.en: The bridge is old, but the tower is new.

cards.more: Think of a see-saw. On one side sits big, on the other small. When you know one side, you know the other. Step 1: learn groß and klein as a team. Step 2: learn alt and neu. Step 3: learn laut and ruhig. Use aber (but) to join two opposites. Extra example: Das Hotel ist klein, aber das Café ist groß.
cards.lead: You can describe places now. On this card: describing words in opposite pairs, like big and small, so you learn two words for the price of one and can contrast places.

deeper.text: Your brain stores opposites together, so say each pair out loud and then use it in a comparing sentence. aber means but, and it joins two ideas with a comma before it. People compare all the time, so pairs like alt and neu are very useful in real chats.

example.de: Die Kirche ist alt, aber das Hotel ist neu.
example.en: The church is old, but the hotel is new.

cards.title: sehr: very
cards.body: sehr means very. Put it right before the adjective. It makes the adjective stronger. sehr never changes, and neither does the adjective.
cards.more: sehr is like a volume knob. Without it the word is normal. With it the word is turned up. Step 1: say the sentence with the adjective: Der Hafen ist groß. Step 2: put sehr right before the adjective. Step 3: say it. Do not put sehr anywhere else. Extra example: Die U-Bahn ist sehr laut. = The underground is very loud.
cards.lead: You know the opposite pairs. On this card: sehr, a small word that makes a describing word stronger, so you can say a place is very big or very beautiful.

deeper.text: Pronunciation tip: German s before a vowel sounds like English z, so sehr sounds like zair, and the ending r is soft. sehr always stands before the adjective, never after it. It is the safe word for very in every situation, from a shop to a letter, so you can use it anywhere.

cards.title: nicht and zu: not and too
cards.body: nicht means not: Der Markt ist nicht groß. zu before an adjective means too: Das Hotel ist zu teuer. Both stand right before the adjective, just like sehr.
cards.more: You have three little helpers that go before an adjective: nicht, sehr and zu. They all work in the same place. Step 1: say the adjective. Step 2: pick a helper: nicht (not), sehr (very) or zu (too). Step 3: put it right before the adjective. Be careful: zu in zu Fuß is a different piece. Here zu means too. Extra example: Der Park ist zu klein. = The park is too small.
cards.lead: Next: two more small words that go before the describing word. On this card: nicht for not and zu for too, so you can say a place is not big or is too loud.

deeper.text: zu hides a small judgement. Too big means it is a problem, so Das Hotel ist zu teuer often means I will not stay there. The same spelling zu also appears in zu Fuß, but the job is different there. Here zu always stands before an adjective and means too.

cards.title: Ask: Wie ist …?
cards.body: Ask what something is like with Wie ist …? The verb ist is part 2. For many things, ask Wie sind …? The answer uses sein + an adjective.

examples.de: Der Hafen ist groß und laut.
examples.en: The harbour is big and loud.

steps: Der Hafen ist groß und laut.
cards.more: Wie ist …? is like asking: tell me about it. You get an answer with describing words. Step 1: ask Wie ist der Hafen? Step 2: answer with the thing, ist and an adjective. Step 3: you can join two adjectives with und. Extra example: Wie ist Hamburg? Hamburg ist sehr schön. = What is Hamburg like? Hamburg is very nice.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: how to ask Wie ist …? and answer with two describing words joined by und, so you can describe a place in a short chat.

deeper.text: Wie ist …? is the everyday way to ask for an opinion about a thing, like Wie ist das Hotel? The answer can be short, such as Sehr schön! If you have two adjectives, und joins them, and the verb is only said once. You do not repeat ist for the second one.

drills.hint: Look at the opposites table.
One thing: ist.
Many things: sind.
Thing, then ist, then the adjective.
After sein the adjective has no ending.

drills.prompt: Das Hotel ist zu teuer. What does it mean?
drills.hint: zu before an adjective means too.
Wie + ist + thing.

answers: Der Hafen ist sehr groß, aber der Park ist klein.
blind.hint: Two sentences joined by aber. sehr goes before groß.

check.hint: nicht goes right before the adjective.

lessons.title: Ask for and give directions: the Sie command
lessons.goal: Ask the way and give directions with polite commands.

grammar.point: The polite command (imperative with Sie): verb first, then Sie
grammar.oneLine: Gehen Sie geradeaus! Verb first + Sie, same form as Sie gehen.

mistake.why: A command starts with the verb, then Sie.

terms.meaning: a command: it tells someone what to do
a sentence that tells a person to do something
excuse me, sorry: it gets attention
pieces for to the: zum Bahnhof, zur Bank. Why comes in chapter 7

cards.title: Before we start: asking the way
cards.body: You are lost in Hamburg. You stop a stranger and ask for the way, and they tell you where to go. Today you learn the polite way to say go straight on and turn left.
steps: You already know: Sie, the polite you, from chapter 1
New today: the polite command, verb first, then Sie
By the end you can: ask the way and understand Gehen Sie geradeaus!

examples.why: New today: verb first, then Sie. It is a polite command.
New today: the same pattern with another verb.

cards.more: A polite command in German is just a small flip. In a statement you say Sie gehen. For a command you swap the two words: Gehen Sie. That is all! It sounds kind because you still say Sie. Think of giving a friendly signpost to a visitor. You will practise asking and giving directions bit by bit in the next cards.

cards.title: A polite command: verb first, then Sie
cards.body: A command tells someone what to do. It is called the imperative. With Sie, put the verb first and Sie right after it. The verb has the same form as Sie gehen. End with !
cards.more: Imagine a statement: Sie gehen geradeaus. You are saying what they do. Now flip the first two words: Gehen Sie geradeaus! Now you are telling them what to do. Step 1: write the statement with Sie. Step 2: swap the verb and Sie, so the verb goes first. Step 3: add an exclamation mark. The verb form stays the same. Extra example: Sie nehmen das Taxi. becomes Nehmen Sie das Taxi!
cards.lead: You can describe places. On this card: how to give a polite command to a stranger, with the verb first and Sie right after it, so you can tell someone what to do.

deeper.text: Why Sie? You use the polite Sie with strangers, like someone you ask for the way. The command is not a new verb form. It is simply the Sie statement turned around: Sie gehen becomes Gehen Sie. The verb moves to the front, Sie follows, and you end with an exclamation mark.

cards.title: Command or question? Look at the end mark
cards.body: A command and a yes/no question both start with the verb. Only the end mark and your voice are different. ! tells, ? asks. Only sein is odd: Seien Sie nett!

examples.why: sein is the odd one. Just learn Seien Sie.

cards.more: Two sentences can look the same but mean different things. The little mark at the end tells you. A question mark means: I want to know. An exclamation mark means: please do it. Step 1: look at the first word. A verb? It is a question or a command. Step 2: look at the end mark. Extra example: Nehmen Sie die U-Bahn? asks. Nehmen Sie die U-Bahn! tells. Only sein is odd, so learn Seien Sie as it is.
cards.lead: Commands look a lot like yes/no questions. On this card: how the end mark tells them apart, plus the one odd command, so you know what you are hearing.

deeper.text: In speech you hear the difference: a question goes up at the end, and a command goes down and sounds firmer. On paper only the end mark shows it. For comparison, a normal sein question looks just like the others. The odd command Seien Sie is only for commands, not for questions.

cards.title: bitte and dann: please and then
cards.body: bitte means please. It makes a command polite. Put it right after Sie, or at the start. dann means then. Use it to give steps one after another.

examples.why: bitte can start the sentence. The verb is still next.

cards.more: Giving a route is like giving steps in a recipe. First do this. Then do that. bitte is the sweet word that makes the command friendly. Step 1: say the command. Step 2: add bitte after Sie for politeness. Step 3: add dann before the next step. Extra example: Gehen Sie geradeaus. Gehen Sie dann links. = Go straight. Then go left.
cards.lead: You can give commands now. On this card: bitte to make a command polite and dann to put steps in order, so your directions sound friendly and clear.

deeper.text: bitte does more than one job: it means please, and also you are welcome. In a command it makes things softer, because a bare command can sound strict. dann can also stand at the very start of a statement. Then the verb is still second, so Sie moves behind it: Dann gehen Sie links.

cards.title: Directions: links, rechts, geradeaus
cards.body: Three direction words: links, rechts, geradeaus. Learn die erste Straße (the first street) and die zweite Straße as pieces. Why erste has an e comes later.

examples.de: Nehmen Sie die zweite Straße rechts!
examples.en: Take the second street on the right!

cards.more: Stand at a crossing and point. Left hand: links. Right hand: rechts. Straight ahead: geradeaus. Step 1: pick the verb: gehen, fahren or nehmen. Step 2: add Sie. Step 3: add the direction. To count streets, use die erste Straße, die zweite Straße. Copy them as they are. Extra example: Nehmen Sie die erste Straße links! = Take the first street on the left.
cards.lead: Next: the words for turning. On this card: left, right and straight on, plus the first and second street, so you can say which way and which street to take.

deeper.text: links, rechts and geradeaus never change, whatever the sentence. The direction usually goes at the end: Nehmen Sie die zweite Straße links means Take the second street on the left. The e in erste and zweite comes from the die-word Straße, and you will see why later. Copy it as a piece now.

example.de: Nehmen Sie die erste Straße links!
example.en: Take the first street on the left!

cards.title: Ask the way: Entschuldigung, … zum / zur …
cards.body: Start with Entschuldigung (excuse me). Then ask Wo ist …? or Wie komme ich zum Bahnhof? zum and zur are pieces: learn zum Bahnhof, zum Museum, zur Bank. Why comes in chapter 7.

examples.en: Excuse me, where is the station?
How do I get to the harbour?
How do I get to the church?

cards.more: Imagine you are lost. First you get attention: Entschuldigung. Then you ask. Wie komme ich … is the whole question: how do I come to … ? Then add where you want to go. The little piece zum or zur comes before the place. Learn them with the place: zum Bahnhof, zur Bank. Extra example: Wie komme ich zum Museum? = How do I get to the museum?
cards.lead: You have the direction words. On this card: how to start politely with Entschuldigung and ask the way with zum or zur, so you can ask for a place like the station.

deeper.text: Wie komme ich zum Bahnhof? is literally How come I to the station? It is the standard polite way to ask, and komme is just kommen with ich. Notice the link with ein and eine: zum goes with der-words and das-words, zur goes with die-words. So the same gender idea comes back again.

example.en: How do I get to the market?

cards.title: A whole route: ask and answer
cards.body: Now put everything together. One person asks the way with Entschuldigung. The other uses Sie commands, bitte and dann. Herr Ali says Sie, because he does not know Mira.

examples.de: Entschuldigung, wie komme ich zum Rathaus?
examples.en: Excuse me, how do I get to the town hall?

examples.de: Gehen Sie geradeaus. Nehmen Sie dann die zweite Straße links.
examples.en: Go straight on. Then take the second street on the left.
The town hall is over there.

steps: Entschuldigung, wie komme ich zum Rathaus?
Nehmen Sie dann die zweite Straße links.
cards.more: A route is a short story with steps. Step 1: say where to start. Step 2: use a command with Sie for each step. Step 3: link the steps with dann. Step 4: end with where the place is. Herr Ali and Mira do not know each other, so they use Sie. Extra example: Gehen Sie links. Nehmen Sie dann das Taxi. = Go left. Then take the taxi.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: a full route from question to answer, using commands, bitte and dann, so you can ask for and give directions in one talk.

deeper.text: Real route directions are short and in order. Listen for the order words: erste, dann, dort. Germans often end by saying where the goal is, and the asker usually says thanks. Herr Ali says Sie because adults who do not know each other say Sie. Say thanks politely at the end.

lessons.title: Months and seasons, long and short vowels
lessons.goal: Say when something happens with im + month or season, and hear long and short vowels.

grammar.point: im + month or season says in that month or season; the verb stays in position 2 when the time comes first
grammar.oneLine: im Januar, im Sommer. Wann …? – Im Mai. Time first: the verb is still part 2.

mistake.why: The verb is always part 2, so ich goes after it.

terms.meaning: one of the twelve parts of the year
one of the four parts of the year: spring, summer, autumn, winter
a vowel you hold, like the a in Staat
a vowel you say quickly, like the a in Stadt

cards.title: Before we start: the months and seasons
cards.body: When is the best time to visit Hamburg? In May, or in summer? Today you say when something happens, using the months and the seasons, and you hear two kinds of vowels.
steps: You already know: am + day, like am Montag, from chapter 2
New today: im + month or season, like im Mai
By the end you can: say Im Mai spiele ich Tennis

examples.why: New today: im + month says in that month.

cards.more: Think of a year as a calendar on the wall. For a day you said am, for a month or a season you say im. It is the same little tag, just a different one. And remember: even when the time comes first, the verb still sits in part 2. You will learn the twelve months, then the four seasons, one step at a time.

cards.title: The twelve months
cards.body: German has twelve months. Learn them in order and say them out loud. Every month is a der-word: der Januar, der Mai. The year is das Jahr.
cards.more: Think of a row of twelve boxes, one for each month. They are in the same order as in English, and many look almost the same: Januar, Juli, August. Step 1: say all twelve in order. Step 2: learn the four that look different: März, Mai, Juni, Oktober. Step 3: remember they are all der-words. Extra example: Der Juli ist ein Monat. = July is a month.
cards.lead: You can give directions and describe places. On this card: the twelve months in order, which are all der-words, so you can talk about when things happen.

deeper.text: Many month names look like English, which helps. März is the odd one: it has an Umlaut ä, and Mar-z ends with a ts sound. Juni and Juli sound almost the same, so stress the first syllable and say each one clearly. Some Germans even say Juno and Julei so nobody mixes them up on the phone.

cards.title: im + month: when?
cards.body: To say in a month, put im before it: im Mai, im Januar. im is one piece. Ask with Wann? (when?). The verb is part 2.

examples.en: When do you come to Hamburg?

cards.more: You know am Montag from chapter 2. For months, German uses im instead of am. Learn im Mai as one block. Step 1: ask Wann? Step 2: answer with im and the month. Step 3: keep the verb in part 2. Why it is im and not am comes in chapter 7. Extra example: Wann kommst du? Ich komme im Juli. = When do you come? I come in July.
cards.lead: You know the months now. On this card: how im goes before a month and how to ask Wann?, so you can say when you come or go.

deeper.text: im is really in and dem squeezed together: in dem becomes im. That is why every month and season takes im. They are all der-words. You will see the full reason in chapter 7. For now just remember: month or season, put im in front, and the month itself never changes.

cards.title: The four seasons
cards.body: There are four seasons, and each is a der-word. Use im before them too: im Frühling, im Sommer, im Herbst, im Winter. Germany, Austria and Switzerland all have the four seasons.

examples.de: Ich bin im Frühling in Hamburg.
examples.en: I am in Hamburg in spring.
We like to swim in summer.

examples.de: Im Herbst fahre ich nach Wien.
examples.en: In autumn I go to Vienna.
examples.why: Time first: the verb is still part 2.

cards.more: A year is a circle of four parts. Spring is the start, when things grow. Summer is warm. Autumn is when leaves fall. Winter is cold. Step 1: learn the four words with der. Step 2: add im to say in the season. Step 3: say the whole sentence. Extra example: Im Winter koche ich gern. = In winter I like to cook.
cards.lead: You can say a month with im. On this card: the four seasons, which are also der-words and also take im, so you can say when something happens in the year.

deeper.text: Spelling and sound: Frühling has the letter ü. Make your lips round as if for oo, and then say ee. It is one letter and one sound, so never write ue in its place. Also notice Herbst, with the sounds rb-s-t together. Say it slowly at first, then faster.

cards.title: Start with the time: the verb stays second
cards.body: You can put im Mai first. Then the verb is still part 2, so the subject moves behind it. It is the same rule as with am Montag in chapter 2.

examples.why: Chair 1 is im Mai: the verb is still part 2.

examples.en: When do you go to Berlin?
examples.why: Question word first, then the verb.

cards.more: Remember the chairs. The verb always sits on chair 2. If you put im Mai on chair 1, the verb stays on chair 2 and ich has to move to chair 3. Step 1: pick what goes on chair 1. Step 2: put the verb on chair 2. Step 3: put everything else after it. Extra example: Im Sommer schwimme ich gern. = In summer I like to swim.
cards.lead: You can say when something happens. On this card: putting the time phrase first while the verb stays in second place, and where the subject goes, so the sentence still works.

deeper.text: Which piece goes first is your choice. The first place is the spotlight, so Im Mai spiele ich Tennis stresses May. Both sentences mean the same. What you must not do is move the verb: Im Mai ich spiele is wrong. The verb stays in part 2, and the subject steps behind it.

cards.title: Hamburg through the year
cards.body: Use im + month or season for events. Hamburg has a big harbour party in May. A big fair, the Dom, takes place in spring, summer and winter. Ask Wann ist …?

examples.en: The harbour birthday is in May.

examples.de: Der Dom in Hamburg ist im Frühling, im Sommer und im Winter.
examples.en: The Dom in Hamburg is in spring, in summer and in winter.

cards.more: Hamburg celebrates its harbour every year in May. The city also has a big fair, the Dom, three times a year. Use these to practise. Step 1: ask Wann ist …? Step 2: answer with the event, ist and im + month or season. Step 3: join two or three times with und. Extra example: Der Weihnachtsmarkt ist im Winter. = The Christmas market is in winter.

rows: im Frühling, im Sommer, im Winter

cards.lead: Next: events in one city. On this card: a few Hamburg events and their times, so you can ask Wann ist …? and name the right month or season.

deeper.text: Careful with a false friend: the Hamburg Dom is not a cathedral. It is a big fair with rides and food. In other cities Dom can mean a big church, but in Hamburg people say Dom for the fair. So when you hear Wann ist der Dom? in Hamburg, someone asks about the fun, not about a service.

example.en: The Christmas market is very beautiful.

cards.title: Long and short vowels
cards.body: A vowel can be long or short. Staat has a long a. Stadt has a short a. The spelling gives a clue. h or a double vowel after it: long. A double consonant or several consonants after it: short.

examples.why: Stadt: d and t after the a: short.
Bahn: ah: long. Compare Bank: nk: short.

cards.more: Say the pair Staat and Stadt out loud. In Staat you hold the a, like in ahhh. In Stadt the a is quick, like a tap. English has this too: think of bean and bin. Step 1: look at the letters after the vowel. Step 2: h, aa, ee, oo or ie: hold it. Step 3: two or more consonants: make it quick. Extra pair: Bahn is long and Bank is short.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. On this card: the spelling clues that tell you whether a vowel is long or short, so you can say words with the right sound.

deeper.text: The rule is not perfect, but it works for most words. In Bahn the h is not spoken. It only stretches the a. Try this drill: say Stadt quick and short, then Staat slow and long. In komme the double m is the clue for a short o. Your ear learns faster than any rule, so say them aloud.

example.de: Ben kommt im Mai nach Hamburg.
example.en: Ben comes to Hamburg in May.

drills.hint: For months, learn im as one piece.
im + the month.

drills.prompt: Which month is the first month of the year?

reading.title: Willkommen in Hamburg
reading.text:
Anna: Hallo, Mira! Willkommen in Hamburg!
Mira: Danke, Anna! Ich komme mit dem Zug aus Wien. Ich bin müde.
Anna: Das ist der Bahnhof. Er ist alt. Hier ist die U-Bahn.
Mira: Was ist das? Ist das ein Kino?
Anna: Nein, das ist kein Kino. Das ist das Rathaus.
Mira: Und das? Ist das eine Bank?
Anna: Nein, das ist keine Bank. Das ist eine Kirche, der Michel.
Mira: Wo ist der Hafen?
Anna: Dort! Ben ist auch dort. Er geht zu Fuß. Wir fahren mit dem Bus.
Mira: Super! Ich habe Zeit und Hunger.

Mira: Und das? Ist das eine Bank?

reading.title: Hamburg im Jahr
reading.text:
Mira: Hamburg ist sehr schön! Der Hafen ist groß, aber er ist laut.
Anna: Ja! Das ist die Elbphilharmonie. Sie ist neu und sehr interessant.
Mira: Und der Michel? Ist er neu?
Anna: Nein, er ist sehr alt. Er ist eine Kirche.
Mira: Ist der Michel weit?
Anna: Nein, er ist nicht weit. Wir gehen zu Fuß.
Mira: Wann ist der Hafengeburtstag?
Anna: Im Mai. Im Sommer fahre ich oft mit dem Fahrrad zum Hafen.
Mira: Und im Winter?
Anna: Im Winter ist der Weihnachtsmarkt. Er ist sehr schön, aber ein bisschen teuer.

listening.title: Wie komme ich zum Rathaus?
listening.script:
Mira: Entschuldigung, Herr Ali. Wie komme ich zum Rathaus?
Herr Ali: Gehen Sie geradeaus. Nehmen Sie dann die erste Straße links.
Mira: Die erste Straße links. Ist das weit?
Herr Ali: Nein, das ist nicht weit. Dort ist eine Kirche, der Michel.
Mira: Danke! Wann ist der Hafengeburtstag?
Herr Ali: Im Mai. Er ist sehr schön, aber laut.
Mira: Super! Auf Wiedersehen, Herr Ali!
Herr Ali: Auf Wiedersehen!
